overview.what_it_is: This lesson develops a systematic approach to PTE Academic Reading multiple-choice items. Learners practise identifying what a prompt requires, predicting the likely answer type, reading efficiently for gist and detail, matching ideas rather than isolated words, eliminating distractors, and proving every selected answer with evidence from the passage.

format_facts.label: Item type 1
format_facts.value: Multiple-choice, choose single answer requires the test taker to select one best response from several options.

format_facts.label: Item type 2
format_facts.value: Multiple-choice, choose multiple answers requires the test taker to select all options that are supported by the passage.

format_facts.label: Item components
format_facts.value: A typical item contains instructions, a reading passage, a prompt, and a set of answer options.

format_facts.label: Prompt styles
format_facts.value: Prompts may use wh-questions, such as why, how, what, or which, or may ask the learner to complete a sentence.

format_facts.label: Reading demands
format_facts.value: Questions may test the main idea, specific details, writer purpose, tone, attitude, organization, inference, vocabulary in context, or supporting examples.

format_facts.label: Answer relationship
format_facts.value: Correct options often paraphrase the passage rather than repeat its exact wording.

scoring_factors.name: Single-answer accuracy
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner can identify the one option that best answers the exact prompt.

scoring_factors.name: Multiple-answer precision
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner can select every supported option while avoiding unsupported or partly true distractors.

scoring_factors.name: Main-idea comprehension
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner can distinguish the central message from examples, explanations, and minor details.

scoring_factors.name: Detailed comprehension
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner can locate and correctly interpret facts, reasons, comparisons, definitions, opinions, and sequences.

scoring_factors.name: Inference and purpose
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner can identify implied meaning, the writer's intention, attitude, or reason for including information.

scoring_factors.name: Contextual vocabulary
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the learner can infer the meaning and function of unfamiliar words from context and word structure.

critical_rules: Answer the exact question asked by the prompt, not a different question suggested by familiar words in the passage.
Do not select an option only because it repeats vocabulary from the text; compare the meaning of the whole option with the passage.
For a single-answer item, choose the option that gives the most complete and accurate response, even when another option is partly true.
For a multiple-answer item, evaluate every option independently and select only those that can be supported by clear textual evidence.
Distinguish the passage's main point from supporting details, examples, causes, effects, and background information.
Treat absolute words such as always, never, completely, only, and all with caution unless the passage clearly supports them.
Use surrounding sentences, word stems, prefixes, and suffixes before guessing the meaning of an unfamiliar word.
Before finalizing an answer, identify the sentence or idea in the passage that proves it.

learning_goals: Identify and label the instructions, passage, prompt, and options in a reading multiple-choice item.
Recognize whether a question requires one answer or multiple answers.
Use wh-words and sentence-completion prompts to predict the required information type.
Skim a passage to identify its topic, main idea, tone, and general organization.
Scan efficiently for names, dates, causes, effects, comparisons, definitions, and other specific details.
Recognize paraphrases and avoid relying on exact word matching.
Explain why a selected option is correct and why each rejected option is a distractor.
Infer unfamiliar vocabulary through context, word families, stems, prefixes, and suffixes.
Group academic vocabulary by theme to predict likely passage content.
Apply a repeatable method under timed reading conditions.

core_method.name: Prompt-to-Proof Method
core_method.summary: Decode the prompt first, predict what kind of information is needed, read strategically, and require textual proof before selecting an answer.

steps.detail: Confirm whether the item requires one answer or multiple answers. Read the instructions carefully because the selection rule changes the decision process.
Underline the question focus, including wh-words, limiting expressions, time references, comparison language, and words such as main, purpose, reason, according to, or suggests.
Decide whether the answer should be a reason, method, person, place, definition, result, opinion, example, comparison, main idea, or inference.
Notice repeated themes, contrasting ideas, extreme wording, categories, and vocabulary that may appear as paraphrases in the passage.
Read topic sentences, the introduction, the conclusion, and repeated ideas to establish the passage's gist and organization.
Search for the section connected to the prompt, then read the relevant sentence together with the sentence before and after it.
Classify each option as supported, contradicted, not mentioned, too broad, too narrow, partly true, or answering the wrong question.
Choose the strongest supported answer or answers, reread the complete prompt with the selection, and confirm that each choice has direct or logically necessary evidence.

core_method.formula: TASK TYPE → PROMPT → PREDICT → PREVIEW → SKIM → SCAN → PROVE → ELIMINATE → SELECT → VERIFY

techniques.name: Wh-word decoding
techniques.purpose: To predict the kind of information the answer must contain before reading the passage closely.
how_to: Circle the wh-word or question phrase.
Translate it into an information category.
Predict common language patterns that may signal the answer.
Reject options that belong to the wrong information category.
techniques.example: In the prompt 'Why was the museum closed during the summer?', why requires a reason. Look for cause language such as because, due to, owing to, or as a result of.
techniques.why_it_matters: It narrows the search and prevents the learner from selecting a true detail that does not answer the question.
techniques.common_error: Choosing an option that states when or how the museum closed instead of explaining why.

techniques.name: Sentence-completion grammar check
techniques.purpose: To use grammar and meaning together when the prompt is an incomplete sentence.
how_to: Read the incomplete sentence without the options.
Predict the grammatical form needed after the final word.
Insert each option mentally.
Check both grammatical fit and textual support.
techniques.example: Prompt: 'The author mentions the experiment in order to ...' The answer should complete an infinitive purpose structure, such as 'illustrate an unexpected effect of rewards.'
techniques.why_it_matters: An option may discuss the same topic but fail to complete the sentence logically or grammatically.
techniques.common_error: Selecting an option because its vocabulary appears in the passage even though the completed sentence does not make sense.

techniques.name: Gist in one line
techniques.purpose: To separate the central message from supporting details.
how_to: Read the title if one is provided.
Read the first and final sentences carefully.
Identify repeated nouns and ideas.
Write or think of a one-line statement beginning with 'The passage mainly explains that ...'
techniques.example: After reading about two types of motivation and their effects, a useful gist statement is: 'The passage explains different forms of motivation and shows that external rewards can produce unexpected effects.'
techniques.why_it_matters: Main-idea questions often contain distractors based on memorable examples rather than the whole passage.
techniques.common_error: Choosing the most interesting example instead of the idea that connects all paragraphs.

techniques.name: Topic-sentence mapping
techniques.purpose: To understand passage organization and find where different ideas are developed.
how_to: Identify the sentence that introduces each paragraph's main idea.
Give each paragraph a two-to-five-word label.
Notice whether later sentences provide examples, causes, contrasts, or results.
Use the labels to locate evidence quickly.
techniques.example: Paragraph 1: 'Two kinds of motivation.' Paragraph 2: 'Unexpected effects of external motivation.'
techniques.why_it_matters: Questions about purpose, organization, and supporting points are easier when the role of each paragraph is clear.
techniques.common_error: Reading every sentence at the same speed without recognizing which sentences control the paragraph.

techniques.name: Paraphrase matching
techniques.purpose: To connect answer options with equivalent meanings in the passage.
how_to: Identify the key meaning in an option.
Look for synonyms, changed word forms, or altered sentence structure in the passage.
Compare the complete proposition, not individual words.
Check whether the option adds, removes, or changes an important condition.
techniques.example: Passage: 'Motivation increases the amount of effort a student invests.' Option: 'Motivated learners devote more energy to their work.' These express the same idea.
techniques.why_it_matters: Correct answers frequently avoid copying the source language directly.
techniques.common_error: Rejecting the correct option because it uses different vocabulary.

techniques.name: Distractor classification
techniques.purpose: To eliminate wrong options using a clear reason rather than intuition.
how_to: Mark an option as supported only when the passage confirms its full meaning.
Mark it contradicted when the passage states the opposite.
Mark it not mentioned when the idea is plausible but absent.
Mark it partly true when only one part is supported.
Mark it wrong focus when it does not answer the prompt.
techniques.example: A passage identifies drought as a present indicator of environmental change. Options such as campaigners, industrial gases, and carbon dioxide may be related to the topic, but they represent people or causes rather than the requested indicator.
techniques.why_it_matters: Most distractors are designed to be related to the passage while failing in one precise way.
techniques.common_error: Rejecting an option as 'wrong' without identifying whether it is contradicted, unsupported, incomplete, or irrelevant.

techniques.name: Evidence-window reading
techniques.purpose: To avoid misinterpreting a keyword found in isolation.
how_to: Locate the key sentence connected to the prompt.
Read at least one sentence before it.
Read at least one sentence after it.
Check pronouns, contrast linkers, conditions, and examples before deciding.
techniques.example: A sentence may say, 'The method was initially successful. However, later trials produced inconsistent results.' Reading only the first sentence would create the wrong answer.
techniques.why_it_matters: Writers often qualify, contrast, or correct an idea in the following sentence.
techniques.common_error: Stopping as soon as a word from an option appears in the passage.

techniques.name: Word-part and context inference
techniques.purpose: To make a careful guess about unfamiliar vocabulary without losing too much time.
how_to: Identify the word's likely part of speech.
Look for a familiar stem or related word.
Identify prefixes and suffixes.
Read nearby definitions, examples, contrasts, and results.
Replace the unknown word with a simple possible meaning and test the sentence.
techniques.example: In 'The policy was ineffective and was therefore discontinued,' the prefix in- suggests 'not,' effect relates to results, and discontinued confirms that the policy did not work.
techniques.why_it_matters: The exact dictionary definition is often unnecessary; an approximate contextual meaning may be enough to answer correctly.
techniques.common_error: Spending too long trying to translate every unfamiliar word.

techniques.name: Theme-vocabulary grouping
techniques.purpose: To activate background vocabulary and predict likely passage content.
how_to: Group related words under a broad academic heading.
Add several synonyms, collocations, and associated concepts.
Predict common text types that might use the group.
Use the group to recognize paraphrases during reading.
techniques.example: Constitution, democracy, self-government, and political landscape belong under Politics or Government. Related words include policy, representation, legislation, and electoral system.
techniques.why_it_matters: Recognizing semantic groups improves reading speed even when the exact wording changes.
techniques.common_error: Memorizing isolated words without learning their relationships, collocations, or typical contexts.

worked_examples.title: Predicting the answer type from a why prompt
worked_examples.input: Passage: 'The city museum closed from December to February so that engineers could replace its outdated electrical system before the main tourist season.' Prompt: 'Why was the museum closed during the summer?' Options: A. Because visitor numbers were low. B. Because its electrical system required replacement. C. Because a new exhibition was being designed. D. Because engineers were unavailable.
worked_examples.decoding: The word why asks for a reason. The answer should identify the cause of the closure, not its timing, duration, or later benefit.
worked_examples.plan: Scan for the sentence containing closed, then identify the purpose clause beginning with 'so that.' Compare the meaning of every option with that clause.
worked_examples.model_answer: B. Because its electrical system required replacement.

annotations.comment: 'Why' signals that the required information is a reason.
The passage directly states that engineers needed to replace the outdated electrical system.
Visitor numbers are not given as the reason.
No new exhibition is mentioned.
The passage says engineers performed the work, not that they were unavailable.

worked_examples.title: Separating an indicator from related climate vocabulary
worked_examples.input: Passage: 'Researchers point to increasingly long droughts and falling river levels as visible indicators of regional climate change. Industrial emissions and rising carbon dioxide concentrations are major causes, while environmental campaigners continue to demand stronger controls.' Prompt: 'Which option is presented as a current indicator of environmental change?' Options: A. Campaigners. B. Industrial emissions. C. Carbon dioxide. D. Drought.
worked_examples.decoding: The key word indicator means a sign or observable evidence. The prompt does not ask for a cause, a person, or a substance.
worked_examples.plan: Classify each option by its role in the passage: campaigners are people, emissions and carbon dioxide are causes, and drought is a visible sign.

annotations.comment: The answer must be an observable sign.
The text explicitly calls long droughts visible indicators.
Industrial emissions and carbon dioxide are strongly related to climate change but are categorized as causes.
Campaigners are people responding to the issue, not indicators of it.

worked_examples.title: Finding the main idea rather than a supporting example
worked_examples.input: Passage: 'Almost all students are motivated in one way or another. Some are interested in demanding academic work, while others are strongly attracted to social activities. Motivation affects effort, persistence, attention, and the value students give to rewards. Because of these effects, motivation generally improves performance.' Prompt: 'What is the writer's main purpose?' Options: A. To criticize students who prefer social activities. B. To explain that motivation has several positive effects on learning and performance. C. To argue that academic motivation is the only useful kind. D. To show that rewards always improve performance.
worked_examples.decoding: The phrase main purpose requires the idea that covers the whole passage. Examples of academic and social motivation support the larger claim about motivation's effects.
worked_examples.plan: Summarize the passage in one sentence, then select the option that matches the full summary without adding judgment or absolute claims.
worked_examples.model_answer: B. To explain that motivation has several positive effects on learning and performance.

annotations.comment: The passage lists several ways motivation influences learning and concludes that it improves performance.
The writer describes socially motivated students but does not criticize them.
The passage accepts more than one kind of motivation.
The absolute word 'always' is unsupported, and rewards are not the passage's central focus.

worked_examples.title: Choosing multiple supported answers
worked_examples.input: Passage: 'Urban trees reduce surface temperatures by providing shade and releasing moisture into the air. They may also improve air quality by trapping some airborne particles. However, trees require long-term maintenance, and poorly selected species can damage pavements or underground pipes.' Prompt: 'According to the passage, which statements are correct?' Options: A. Urban trees can help cool cities. B. All tree species improve underground infrastructure. C. Trees may capture some particles from the air. D. Urban trees require no maintenance. E. Inappropriate species may cause structural damage.
worked_examples.decoding: The instruction requires multiple answers. Each option must be evaluated separately against the passage.
worked_examples.plan: Match each option to a specific sentence. Reject options containing reversed or absolute meanings.

annotations.comment: Supported by shade and moisture reducing surface temperatures.
Contradicted because some species can damage pipes.
Supported by the statement that trees can trap airborne particles.
Contradicted by the requirement for long-term maintenance.
Supported by the warning about pavement and pipe damage.

worked_examples.title: Inferring an unfamiliar word from context
worked_examples.input: Passage: 'The first trial produced promising results, but the improvement was transient. Within two weeks, participants had returned to their previous performance levels.' Prompt: 'The word transient is closest in meaning to:' Options: A. Permanent. B. Temporary. C. Unexpected. D. Measurable.
worked_examples.decoding: The second sentence explains that the improvement disappeared within two weeks, so the unknown adjective describes something that did not last.
worked_examples.plan: Use the contrast between promising results and the later return to previous levels. Replace transient with each option and test the meaning.

annotations.comment: Participants returned to their earlier level after only two weeks.
The improvement lasted for a short period.
Permanent expresses the opposite meaning.
The result may have been unexpected or measurable, but neither word explains its short duration.

items.when_to_use: Use this as a reminder to select only information explicitly supported by the text, not outside knowledge.
Use it to identify the broad idea covering most or all of the passage.

items.item: The writer mentions X in order to
items.when_to_use: Use it to identify the function of an example, fact, quotation, or comparison.
Use it when the answer is not directly stated but follows logically from textual evidence.

items.item: Which of the following is supported
items.when_to_use: Use it to test each option against direct or logically necessary evidence.

items.item: The word X is closest in meaning to
items.when_to_use: Use it to infer meaning from context rather than choose the word's most familiar dictionary definition.
Look for these when a why prompt requires a reason.

items.item: due to / owing to / as a result of
items.when_to_use: Use these to identify noun phrases expressing causes.
Look after these words for conclusions or results.
Use these to map cause-and-effect relationships.

items.item: because of this / for this reason
items.when_to_use: Use these to connect earlier evidence with a later conclusion.
Read carefully after this word because the writer may limit or reverse the previous idea.
Use these to distinguish a concession from the writer's main claim.
Use these to identify comparisons or differences between two subjects.
Look for a correction, limitation, or unexpected contrast.
Use these to identify a result that occurs contrary to an expected condition.
Use it to identify the writer's preferred or corrected alternative.
Recognize that the following information supports a broader point and may not itself be the main idea.
Use it to identify members of a category or examples of a general statement.
Use it to recognize a non-complete list of supporting details.
Use it to identify evidence provided to clarify or prove a claim.
Use it to identify a detail receiving special emphasis.
Label an option this way when its complete meaning matches direct or logically necessary evidence.
Use this when the text states the opposite of the option.
Use this when an option is plausible but has no textual evidence.
Use this when one part of an option is supported but another part is wrong or missing.
Use this when an option makes a larger claim than the passage supports.
Use this when an option describes only one example but the prompt asks for the main idea.
Use this when the option is true but does not match the information category requested by the prompt.
Use these to recognize that the writer views a result as contrary to expectations.
Use these to identify a negative evaluation.
Use these to identify strong confidence or certainty.
Use these to recognize limited certainty and avoid selecting an overly definite option.
Use these to identify a cautious or debatable claim.

common_mistakes.mistake: Selecting an option because it repeats exact words from the passage.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Distractors often copy visible vocabulary while changing the relationship, category, cause, time, or conclusion.
common_mistakes.fix: Paraphrase the option in simple language and compare its complete meaning with the passage.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading the passage without first understanding the prompt.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The learner reads without a clear purpose and may remember information that does not answer the question.
common_mistakes.fix: Decode the prompt and predict the required answer type before close reading.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming the passage must always be read before the prompt and options.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A fixed reading order may waste time and prevent focused scanning.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a flexible order: inspect the instructions and prompt first, preview options briefly, then skim and scan the passage.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing a supporting detail for a main-idea question.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A memorable example may be accurate but too narrow to represent the passage as a whole.
common_mistakes.fix: Create a one-sentence summary and choose the option that covers the greatest proportion of the passage.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Multiple-choice options must be correct as complete statements; one unsupported phrase makes the whole option unreliable.
common_mistakes.fix: Break long options into claims and verify every claim separately.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using personal knowledge instead of passage evidence.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: An option may be generally true in real life but still be unsupported by the supplied text.
common_mistakes.fix: Ask, 'Where is the proof in this passage?' and reject answers based only on outside knowledge.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignoring negative or limiting words in the prompt.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Words such as not, except, least, mainly, only, and most likely can reverse or narrow the required answer.
common_mistakes.fix: Underline all limiting words before examining the options.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating all related vocabulary as the same category.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A passage may distinguish between a cause, effect, indicator, example, person, and solution even when all belong to the same topic.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the role of each option in relation to the prompt.

common_mistakes.mistake: Stopping at the first sentence containing a matching keyword.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The next sentence may introduce contrast, exception, or qualification.
common_mistakes.fix: Read an evidence window containing the sentence before and after the match.

common_mistakes.mistake: Selecting too many options in a multiple-answer item.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Related, plausible, or partly true distractors may be included alongside fully supported answers.
common_mistakes.fix: Require independent textual proof for every selected option and remove any option that cannot be fully defended.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to understand every unfamiliar word.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: This consumes time and interrupts understanding of the passage's main structure.
common_mistakes.fix: Decide whether the word is essential; when it is, infer only the approximate meaning needed for the question.

time_budget.focus: Label instructions, passage, prompt, and options; distinguish single-answer from multiple-answer items.
Classify wh-prompts and sentence-completion prompts by the information they require.
Build theme-related word groups and predict likely synonyms, collocations, and passage content.
Identify titles, topic sentences, repeated concepts, paragraph functions, and the overall gist.
Locate details efficiently and read evidence windows around relevant keywords.
Classify options as supported, contradicted, not mentioned, partly true, too broad, too narrow, or wrong focus.
Complete mixed single-answer and multiple-answer items using the full Prompt-to-Proof Method.
Record the reason for each error and identify one strategy to apply in the next practice set.

drills.name: Prompt category sprint
drills.instructions: Read ten prompts without passages. For each prompt, write the required answer type, such as reason, method, comparison, main idea, purpose, definition, detail, or inference.

drills.name: Five-second gist
drills.instructions: Read the title and topic sentence of each paragraph, then state the passage's likely main idea in one sentence before reading the details.

drills.name: Paragraph label drill
drills.instructions: Give each paragraph a short functional label such as definition, cause, example, contrast, problem, solution, or conclusion.

drills.name: Paraphrase pairs
drills.instructions: Match sentences from a passage with answer options that express the same meaning using different vocabulary or grammar.

drills.name: Distractor autopsy
drills.instructions: For every wrong option, identify one exact failure type: contradicted, not mentioned, partly true, too broad, too narrow, extreme, or wrong question.

drills.name: Evidence underline
drills.instructions: Underline the shortest passage segment that proves each correct answer and circle any limiting word that makes a distractor wrong.

drills.name: Unknown-word detective
drills.instructions: For each unfamiliar word, identify its part of speech, stem, affixes, nearby clues, and approximate contextual meaning.

drills.name: Theme-group expansion
drills.instructions: Organize vocabulary into topics such as population, politics, environment, education, health, technology, and economics, then add five related academic terms to each group.

drills.name: Multiple-answer restraint
drills.instructions: Complete several multiple-answer questions and write one evidence sentence beside every selected option. Remove any choice that lacks clear proof.

practice_plan.routine: For each practice item, spend the opening stage identifying the task type, underlining the prompt focus, and predicting the answer category. Skim for the passage's structure, scan for the relevant section, and read a small evidence window closely. Evaluate every option with a named reason, select only fully supported answers, and finish by rereading the prompt together with the selected response. After checking the answer, record whether any error came from prompt decoding, locating evidence, misunderstanding vocabulary, confusing main ideas with details, or accepting a distractor.

mastery_checklist: I can distinguish between choose-single-answer and choose-multiple-answers instructions.
I can label the instructions, passage, prompt, and options in a multiple-choice item.
I can identify the important wh-word or limiting phrase in a prompt.
I can predict whether the answer should be a reason, process, comparison, detail, purpose, inference, or main idea.
I can skim a passage and state its gist in one sentence.
I can identify the topic sentence and supporting function of each paragraph.
I can scan for specific facts, definitions, causes, effects, examples, and sequences.
I can recognize correct paraphrases even when they use different vocabulary from the passage.
I can identify textual evidence for every answer I select.
I can explain why each rejected option is wrong.
I can distinguish a cause from an effect, indicator, example, person, or solution.
I can detect options that are too broad, too narrow, extreme, or only partly true.
I can infer an unfamiliar word's approximate meaning from context and word parts.
I can group academic vocabulary by theme and use those groups to predict content.
I can complete mixed multiple-choice items using a consistent timed routine.
strategy_notes: The best starting point is usually the instructions and prompt because they define the reading purpose.
Previewing options should be brief; do not spend so long analyzing them that they distort your understanding of the passage.
For a main-idea question, prioritize ideas repeated or developed across the passage rather than a single striking sentence.
For a detail question, locate the relevant area and read locally instead of repeatedly rereading the entire passage.
For a writer-purpose question, ask what function a sentence or example performs: defining, illustrating, contrasting, criticizing, supporting, or concluding.
For an inference question, choose the conclusion that must or reasonably can follow from the passage, not one that is merely possible.
Correct options often preserve the passage's degree of certainty. If the text says may, an option saying always is probably too strong.
The presence of familiar vocabulary is not evidence; the relationship between ideas must also match.
In multiple-answer items, do not search for a predetermined number of answers. Judge every option independently.
When two options appear possible in a single-answer item, compare scope, precision, and completeness; the stronger answer usually covers the prompt more exactly.
A correct answer may combine information from more than one sentence, especially in main-idea, inference, and purpose questions.
Vocabulary groups are most useful when they include related concepts, collocations, word families, and common text types rather than isolated translations.
Maintain an error log using categories such as wrong prompt interpretation, keyword matching, missed contrast, unsupported inference, vocabulary error, and over-selection.
Speed should come from a repeatable process and selective reading, not from rushing through every sentence.
